title: Social Contract Theory: Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau on Political Authority
excerpt: A comparative Political Science guide to three classic social-contract traditions: security under Hobbes, rights and consent under Locke, and freedom through the general will under Rousseau.

sections.heading: Why social contract theory matters
paragraphs: Social contract theory asks how political authority can be justified by reference to agreement or consent rather than simply inherited status or force. The tradition is central to modern political thought, but Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau use the contract idea for very different purposes. Treating them as if they proposed the same theory is a common examination mistake. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy describes contractarian approaches as theories in which the legitimacy of political authority is connected to agreement among those subject to collectively enforced arrangements. For Political Science, the best method is comparative: identify each thinker’s view of the pre-political condition, the problem that motivates political society, what individuals authorize or retain, and the kind of political order that results.

sections.heading: Hobbes: security and undivided authority
paragraphs: Thomas Hobbes develops the contract as a solution to insecurity in the absence of a common authority capable of enforcing peace. His political argument is associated with authorization of a powerful sovereign whose central task is to secure order. The Stanford Encyclopedia notes that Hobbes used social-contract reasoning to defend an absolute, undivided sovereign power. The analytical point is that fear of violent conflict and the need for predictable enforcement make political authority rational in his framework. Hobbes therefore gives priority to security and effective sovereignty. This does not mean every act of government becomes morally admirable; it means his theory sets a very high threshold for challenging the authority that prevents a return to destructive insecurity.

sections.heading: Locke: natural rights and limited government
paragraphs: John Locke begins from natural freedom and equality and argues that individuals possess rights, including life, liberty and property, independently of particular governments. Political society is formed so those rights can be enjoyed more securely under known laws and impartial institutions. Government is therefore fiduciary and limited: it exists for public purposes and rests on consent. The Stanford Encyclopedia emphasizes that, for Locke, people conditionally transfer some rights to government while retaining others, and government that fundamentally fails its trust can be resisted and replaced. Compared with Hobbes, Locke gives much greater constitutional significance to limited authority, rights and the continuing standards by which rulers may be judged.

sections.heading: Rousseau: freedom and the general will
paragraphs: Jean-Jacques Rousseau frames the problem differently: how can people live under political authority while remaining free? His Social Contract makes the general will central to legitimate political order. The general will is not simply whatever a temporary majority happens to want; it concerns citizens considered collectively and oriented toward the common good. Rousseau’s theory therefore links sovereignty with popular membership in the law-making community. For comparison, Hobbes emphasizes peace through sovereign authority, Locke emphasizes rights-protecting government based on consent, and Rousseau emphasizes political freedom through collective self-rule. A strong answer should compare assumptions, purpose of contract, sovereignty, rights, resistance and freedom, then conclude that the shared contract device produces sharply different theories of legitimate government.
